summary: Provides guidance to authors and reviewers of new protocols and extensions on considering operations and management from the start. Retrofitting manageability later is harder, so it offers a checklist of questions to address. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you build a machine, you should think about how people will fix and run it. This document gives protocol designers a list of such questions to ask early.

questions: how to consider operations and management in new protocols
what is the ops and management checklist for protocol design
what is a manageability considerations section
why should protocols be designed for operations and management
what is the difference between an information model and a data model
subtitle: A checklist of operations and management questions that protocol designers should answer before a protocol ships.

tldr.problem: New protocols are often designed without enough thought for how they will be deployed, operated and managed, and retrofitting that later is hard.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives guidelines on operational considerations and management considerations (fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security), advice on documenting them, and a review checklist in Appendix A.
tldr.outcome: The guidance is advisory, not an interoperability standard: it deliberately avoids RFC 2119 keywords and does not require any specific management protocol.

facts.label: Counter guideline
facts.value: One counter per critical section per layer

facts.label: Placement
facts.value: Manageability section immediately before Security Considerations

today: RFC 5706 is Informational and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a set of guidelines, not a standard.

sections.title: Why Design for Operations
sections.content:
Retrofitting operations and management mechanisms is often hard and architecturally unpleasant, and some design choices make deployment, operations and management especially hard. RFC 5706 asks protocol designers and working groups to consider these needs early, document how they could be met and suggest, preferably standard, management protocols and data models. The analogy it draws is to security: consider which threats are relevant, document mitigations.

The RFC separates operational considerations (running the protocol in a network, even with no management protocol in use) from management considerations (management protocols and data models). It does not impose a solution. A designer may conclude that proprietary command line interfaces are enough, but that should be an explicit decision rather than an omission.

The motivation is that the IETF Standard Management Framework (SNMP, SMIv2 and MIB modules) proved inadequate as the only approach, and the policy of requiring a MIB module is being replaced by one open to several protocols and data models.
sections.plainLanguage: It is much easier to add a door when you draw the house than after the walls are up. Think about the door first.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Operational aspects have a serious impact on a protocol's success: bad interactions with existing solutions, a difficult upgrade path, hard debugging, or a state diagram that operators find hard to understand. The RFC's example is BGP flap damping, which caused false damping and lost reachability when path exploration was not considered, so many networks turned it off.

  • Operation and setup: say how the protocol works out of the box, give sensible, conservative defaults, and make all actual values retrievable.
  • Migration path: consider coexistence with older versions and incremental deployment.
  • Requirements on other protocols: RSVP unintentionally needed routers to inspect packets, which led to the router alert option.
  • Impact on the network: scaling, traffic patterns, and infrastructure such as DNS and routing tables.
  • Verifying operation: plan active and passive tests and simple health indicators.
sections.plainLanguage: Think about how people will set it up, upgrade it, and tell whether it works, and whether it bothers the other machines nearby.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
Management should start from identifying what is to be managed and how it is installed, configured and monitored. The RFC warns that the classic MIB approach tends to cover one endpoint on one device, not the protocol across both ends or the whole service, quoting RFC 3535 that MIB modules are often a list of ingredients without a recipe.

Interoperability matters at the syntactic and semantic level. Information models, written in English text, focus on what is gathered, for example which errors share one counter, so the number means the same whether read via SNMP, CLI or syslog. Models should keep configuration, operational state and statistics distinct, and start from a small set of essential objects.

The RFC then walks through areas: fault (liveness, fault determination, root cause analysis, isolation), configuration (defaults, ordered data such as ACLs, network-wide changes, dump and restore, minimal change from configuration A to B), accounting, performance (protocol, device, network and service monitoring, with clear counter definitions) and security (logs, access control, secure transport).
sections.plainLanguage: Check how to watch it, fix it, change its settings, count its use and keep it safe, and make a counter mean the same thing everywhere.

sections.title: Documenting the Considerations
sections.content:
Documents should include a Manageability Considerations section covering the topics in the RFC. When a topic does not apply, it is useful to say briefly why. If a protocol truly needs no management functionality, the recommended text is a simple statement such as 'There are no new manageability requirements introduced by this document', with a short explanation. For an extension, point to the base document's considerations.

The section is recommended to sit immediately before the Security Considerations section, so reviewers and tools can find it easily.

The RFC deliberately does not use the RFC 2119 capitalized keywords. Words such as 'must' or 'should' carry their natural English meaning only, because the document does not define interoperability requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Write down what you thought about, even if it is 'nothing needed here, because...'. Put it in the same place every time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says it introduces no new security concerns, but notes trade-offs. A management portal is a doorway for attack, so only management protocols with adequate authentication, message integrity checking and authorization should be used. A standard description of manageable knobs also tells an attacker what to try to control.

A manageable, inspectable protocol gives operators a better chance of spotting and quarantining attacks, but easy inspection is a risk if the wrong person inspects. Excess security events could even be used to flood logs and alerts.
sections.plainLanguage: A control panel helps the owner fix things, but a thief would love it too, so lock it. Too many alarm bells can also be used to annoy you.

sections.title: The Review Checklist
sections.content: Appendix A turns the guidance into questions that reviewers are expected to ask, grouped as Operational Considerations (A.1), Management Considerations (A.2) and Documentation (A.3). Examples from A.1 include: has deployment been discussed, is the specification deployable and does it scale, does each configuration parameter have a reasonable default, how will devices and managers find and authenticate each other, and are there backward compatibility issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The back of the document is a quiz you can run on your design before showing it to reviewers.
